sections.h2: Trenton tax offices and phone numbers
sections.html:
Billing, valuing and appeals sit in three different places. The Division of Tax sends bills and takes payments, the Tax Assessor puts a value on each parcel, and the Mercer County Board of Taxation hears disputes. Questions about a valuation belong with the assessor.

  • Division of Tax (billing, payments, delinquent notices, the annual tax sale): 609-989-3070.
  • Tax Assessor (value, deductions, exemptions, appeal forms): 609-989-3083.
  • Mercer County Board of Taxation, McDade Administration Building, 640 South Broad Street, Room 317, Trenton: 609-989-6704.

The Division of Tax also keeps records, files the reports state law requires, and prepares lists of properties for tax foreclosure.

sections.h2: Trenton housing and who owns it
sections.html:
Trenton is mostly renters, in a compact capital city. The 2020 census counted 90,871 residents and the 2025 estimate is 91,506, living on 7.58 square miles of land. Value and housing type shift from one ward to the next, so a figure for the whole city is only a starting point. A seller here is often dealing with a rowhouse or older single family home on a small lot, sometimes with a tenant inside.

The Division of Tax lists deductions for permanently disabled owners, seniors and veteran owners who meet income and residency tests, and the assessor's office issues the applications.

Installments fall on the first day of four months: February, May, August and November. Ten days of grace follow each one before a balance turns delinquent. Trenton does not use the July mailing pattern of calendar year towns. The city mails bills twice a year.

  • Late June or early July: bills for the August and November quarters.
  • Late December or early January: bills for the February and May quarters.

The first-half bills are preliminary, based on about half of the prior year's taxes. When the second-half bill is issued it uses the current year's rate, and the preliminary amount is subtracted from the full-year total. That is why the winter quarters can look different from the summer ones even when the assessment has not moved.

Delinquent balances accrue 8% a year up to $1,500 and 18% beyond that, measured from the opening day of the quarter once grace runs out. Once a delinquency has used up the $1,500 tier, later delinquencies are charged at 18% until the account balance returns to zero.

A 6% penalty may also be added to a delinquency above $10,000 that is still open at the end of the fiscal year. Partial payments are accepted under the same interest terms. For a receipt, mail a stamped return envelope with the stub; otherwise the canceled check serves as proof.

A municipal tax bill or charge still unpaid on May 11 is open to the tax sale, provided the sale takes place before the fiscal year ends on June 30. From May 11 until the sale, payments must be made by certified check, cash or money order.

The rule is the same every year, and the Division of Tax holds the sale annually. An owner who plans to sell with taxes behind should clear the balance or have the payoff figure ready before May 11, because a lien adds a separate redemption step to the closing.

Each year, April 1 closes the window for ordinary appeals and December 1 closes it for added or omitted assessments. Both go to the Mercer County Board of Taxation. If your assessment exceeds $1,000,000 you may file directly with the New Jersey Tax Court, and a decision from the county board can be taken to Tax Court within 45 days.

A copy of the petition is served on the board at 640 South Broad Street, and the municipal assessor and municipal clerk each get one too. The board does not accept faxes or emailed copies. Its appeal page also offers an appeal checklist, appeal reminders and a comparable sales analysis form. If you have recent sale prices for similar homes nearby, attach them. The owner carries the burden of showing the assessment is out of line with market value.

sections.h2: Passing the bill to the buyer
sections.html:
A bill belongs with the new owner after a sale, and a fee may apply to a duplicate. Before the closing date, ask the Division of Tax what is paid and what is open, since delinquency interest runs back to the start of the quarter.

Flood zone status is also worth checking when you list a home near the Delaware River. If a municipality qualifies for federal flood insurance, an owner who does not buy it can be denied federal disaster assistance. The Municipal Clerk can tell you whether a property lies in a flood zone.

Bring the latest tax bill, any deduction approval letter, and the assessor's notice of value. Ask the Division of Tax for a statement showing which quarters are paid. If a balance is open, ask for the payoff in writing, and make sure it is current through the closing date. Remember that the preliminary and final bills differ, so a buyer who sees only the winter figure may expect a bigger summer bill.

Keep copies of every payment receipt or canceled check for the current year. If you rent the house to a tenant, tell the buyer early, since occupancy affects timing and how the current quarter is divided. A cash buyer who purchases as is will still want the tax picture, but can usually work around an open balance by paying it at closing out of your proceeds.

Owing tax does not stop a sale. The closing agent pays the balance out of your proceeds, and the Division of Tax can give a written figure for the day of closing. Interest keeps running until the account is paid, so a late closing costs more. If the balance has already been sold as a lien after May 11, the buyer's title company will also need the redemption step finished before the deed can pass cleanly.

Owners who plan ahead can call 609-989-3070 early in the process, ask for the account history, and confirm that preliminary and final bills have both been credited. That one call prevents most last-minute surprises.

faqs.q: What number reaches Trenton's tax staff?
faqs.a: Call the Division of Tax at 609-989-3070. Assessment and deduction questions go to the Assessor at 609-989-3083. The collection office does not answer value questions.

faqs.q: What is the grace period for Trenton property tax?
faqs.a: Ten days after the first of February, May, August or November. After that, taxes are delinquent and interest is counted from the first day of the quarter.

faqs.q: When is the Trenton tax appeal deadline?
faqs.a: April 1 for ordinary assessments and December 1 for added or omitted ones. The Mercer County Board of Taxation takes the filing, and an assessment above $1,000,000 can go straight to Tax Court.

faqs.q: Why do my first-half and second-half Trenton bills differ?
faqs.a: The winter bill is a preliminary figure near half of last year's taxes. The summer bill applies the new rate for the year and subtracts the preliminary amount already billed.

faqs.q: Can Trenton sell a lien if I have owed tax for a long time?
faqs.a: Yes. A bill unpaid on May 11 can be sold, provided the sale happens before June 30. After May 11 the city takes only certified funds, cash or a money order.
